c.tagline: Chaotic, soulful bayfront city where pizza was born under Vesuvius.

taxi.fareNote: Taxis are metered, but fixed 'tariffe predeterminate' apply on common routes (about €21 airport-Centrale, €24 airport-port); ask for the fare predeterminata and confirm it before setting off.

emergency.note: 112 is the EU-wide emergency number connecting to police, fire, and ambulance; 113 reaches state police and 118 reaches medical emergencies directly.

solo.f: generally fine; watch for petty theft

avoid.reason: Pickpocketing and scooter bag-snatching; caution in the Spanish Quarters, Forcella and Sanità.
Around Piazza Garibaldi/the central station is best avoided late at night.

hood_desc: The UNESCO-listed historic core threaded by Spaccanapoli and Via dei Tribunali, packed with churches, the Duomo, Cappella Sansevero, street food, and Naples' oldest pizzerias; best for first-timers who want the city's atmosphere on their doorstep.

Naples' elegant, leafy seafront district with the Villa Comunale gardens, designer boutiques, aperitivo bars, and Bay of Naples views; suits travelers wanting upscale dining, shopping, and nightlife within walking distance.

A polished residential hilltop reached by funicular, crowned by Castel Sant'Elmo and the Certosa di San Martino, with sweeping panoramas, cafes, and a calmer pace; good for longer stays and travelers wanting views and quiet.
The classic seafront strip along Via Partenope and Borgo Marinari, anchored by the Castel dell'Ovo and grand Belle Epoque hotels; a romantic, relaxed base right on the water.

The dense grid of narrow lanes climbing off Via Toledo, famous for laundry-strung alleys, street food, the Maradona mural, and vibrant local life; an atmospheric, budget-friendly base close to everything.

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink, though many locals prefer bottled.

transit.hours: Metro Line 1 and the funiculars run roughly 6:00 AM to 11:00 PM (later on Friday and Saturday); a limited night bus network covers the gap after they close.
transit.note: Getting around blends ANM's Metro Line 1, four funiculars up to Vomero, buses and trams, plus Trenitalia's Metro Line 2; EAV's Circumvesuviana line from Napoli Centrale reaches Pompeii, Herculaneum, and Sorrento.
transit.pay: A single ANM ticket is €1.50 and the 90-minute integrated TIC ticket is €1.80 (valid across metro, funiculars, buses and Line 2), sold at tobacconists, machines, and stations. Tap & Go contactless (about €1.10) works on Metro Line 1 at Centrale, Chiaia, and Montesanto and on the Alibus.

transit.m: Alibus shuttle to Napoli Centrale / port (~15-35 min)
Taxi fixed fare to Napoli Centrale

tip.r: Not obligatory; a cover charge (coperto) is often on the bill, so rounding up or leaving a few euros for good service is appreciated but not expected.

food.name: Pizza napoletana
food.desc: Soft, blistered 60-second pizza from a wood oven, in only two true versions: marinara with tomato, garlic and oregano, or margherita.

places.name: L'Antica Pizzeria da Michele
places.note: Serving since 1870 with just two pizzas on the menu; take a ticket and wait.

places.name: Gino e Toto Sorbillo
places.note: The best-known name on pizza street; huge, thin-centred pies.

places.name: 50 Kalo
places.note: Ciro Salvo's high-hydration dough, lighter and more refined than the classics.

food.name: Pizza fritta
food.desc: Deep-fried calzone stuffed with ricotta, provola, pork cicoli and tomato. A post-war survival food that became a Naples signature.

places.name: Pizzeria Starita a Materdei
places.note: Historic pizzeria whose fried montanara appeared in a Sophia Loren film.

places.name: La Masardona
places.note: Family fried-pizza specialists for three generations; nothing else on the menu.

places.name: Zia Esterina Sorbillo
places.note: Fast counter for fried pizza to eat walking, with branches near Piazza Trieste.

food.name: Cuoppo
food.desc: Paper cone of hot fried food: anchovies, squid, potato croquettes, panzarotti and zeppoline, salted and eaten on the move.

places.name: Friggitoria Vomero
places.note: Neighbourhood frying shop that locals rate for a classic land-and-sea cuoppo.

places.name: Friggitoria Fiorenzano
places.note: In the middle of the raucous Pignasecca market, frying since the 1800s.

places.name: Passione di Sofi
places.note: Popular stop on Via dei Tribunali for frittatina and fried snacks.

food.name: Ragu napoletano and genovese
food.desc: Two long-cooked Sunday sauces: ragu of beef and pork simmered for hours in tomato, and genovese, a sweet onion-and-beef sauce despite the name.

places.name: Tandem
places.note: Small chain built entirely around ragu, including a meatball sandwich version.

places.name: Trattoria da Nennella
places.note: Loud, cheap, theatrical set-menu trattoria; cash only and no bookings.

places.name: Trattoria San Ferdinando
places.note: Quieter old-school kitchen near Teatro San Carlo with daily home-style plates.

food.name: Sfogliatella
food.desc: Pastry filled with semolina, ricotta and candied peel, either in crisp shell-shaped riccia layers or soft shortcrust frolla.

places.name: Sfogliatelle Attanasio
places.note: Chaotic alley bakery selling them straight from the oven all morning.

places.name: Pasticceria Pintauro
places.note: The shop credited with bringing the recipe into Naples in the early 1800s.

places.name: Scaturchio
places.note: 1905 pasticceria with pavement tables in the historic centre.

food.name: Baba al rum
food.desc: Mushroom-shaped yeast cake soaked in rum syrup, sometimes split and filled with cream or wild strawberries.

places.name: Scaturchio
places.note: One of the city's benchmark baba, alongside its chocolate ministeriale.

places.name: Gran Caffe Gambrinus
places.note: Grand 1860 cafe by the Royal Palace; pricey but the pastry case is a museum.

places.name: Pasticceria Capparelli
places.note: Old-fashioned counter in the centre, generous and much cheaper than the grand cafes.

food.name: Caffe napoletano
food.desc: Short, dark, thick espresso served pre-sweetened unless you say otherwise. Drunk standing at the bar in seconds, often with a glass of water.

places.name: Gran Caffe Gambrinus
places.note: Historic literary cafe; ask about the caffe sospeso, the pay-it-forward coffee.

places.name: Caffe Mexico
places.note: Local benchmark for a proper Neapolitan espresso; specify amaro for unsweetened.

places.name: Caffe del Professore
places.note: Known for the hazelnut nocciolato and other flavoured Neapolitan coffees.

food.name: Limoncello
food.desc: Bright lemon liqueur made from the peel of Sorrento and Amalfi lemons, kept in the freezer and poured ice-cold after a meal.

places.name: Limone
places.note: Small producer near Piazza San Domenico offering tastings of house limoncello.

places.name: Gran Caffe Gambrinus
places.note: Classic end-of-meal pour in grand surroundings, with pastries to match.

landmarks: Naples Cathedral (Duomo di San Gennaro)
This grand Gothic cathedral houses vials of San Gennaro's blood, which believers say liquefies annually in a beloved and closely watched miracle.
Castel dell'Ovo
Perched on a tiny islet in the Bay of Naples, this ancient seafront castle offers postcard-perfect views and centuries of legend about a magical egg.
Castel Nuovo (Maschio Angioino)
This imposing medieval royal castle, guarded by a striking Renaissance triumphal arch, has dominated Naples' harbor skyline since the 13th century.
Teatro di San Carlo
Europe's oldest continuously active opera house dazzles with gilded interiors and world-class performances, predating even Milan's La Scala.
Piazza del Plebiscito
Naples' grandest public square, framed by the curved colonnade of San Francesco di Paola and the Royal Palace, is the heart of the historic center.
Spaccanapoli
This narrow, dead-straight street literally 'splits Naples' in two, brimming with shrines, shops, and centuries-old street life in the historic quarter.
Certosa di San Martino
This former Carthusian monastery perched on a hill offers baroque splendor, panoramic views over the entire Bay of Naples, and a fascinating city museum.
Galleria Umberto I
This elegant 19th-century glass-domed shopping arcade near the Teatro di San Carlo is a stunning showcase of Neapolitan architecture and elegance.
Cappella Sansevero
A Baroque chapel near Piazza San Domenico Maggiore holding Giuseppe Sanmartino's hyperrealistic marble sculpture, the Veiled Christ, alongside a crypt of anatomical curiosities.
Catacombe di San Gennaro
Naples's oldest Christian catacombs, an underground network of tombs and frescoes that became a pilgrimage site after the saint's remains were interred there.

train.note: No international train starts in Naples, so any trip abroad means changing in Rome or Milan - the most useful link is the ÖBB Nightjet sleeper from Rome Tiburtina to Munich and Vienna, which you reach with a 70-minute Frecciarossa from Napoli Centrale. Domestically Trenitalia and its rival Italo run frequent high-speed services from Napoli Centrale, with Rome in about 1h10, Florence around 3 hours and Milan about 4h30. EAV's narrow-gauge Circumvesuviana, from the lower level of the same station, is the line for Herculaneum, Pompeii Scavi and Sorrento; it is cheap and frequent but slow, crowded and a known spot for pickpockets. High-speed fares work like air fares, so book ahead, while Circumvesuviana tickets are simply bought at the machine.

bus.note: Long-distance coaches use the Metropark terminal on Corso Arnaldo Lucci, directly behind Napoli Centrale, with a smaller set of stops at Piazza Garibaldi. FlixBus is the operator for international journeys, generally sold as through tickets with a change in northern Italy, while Itabus (https://www.itabus.it/en) and FlixBus between them cover the domestic long-distance network to Rome, Bari, Milan and Turin. Coaches are markedly cheaper than the high-speed trains but take two to three times as long. Book online; the terminal has no proper ticket hall.

ferry.note: Naples is one of the Mediterranean's busiest passenger ports and everything sails from the waterfront a 10-15 minute walk from Piazza Municipio: fast hydrofoils from Molo Beverello, car ferries from Calata Porta di Massa a few hundred metres east, and the big overnight ships from the Stazione Marittima. Capri is about 50 minutes by hydrofoil or 80 by ferry, Ischia around an hour, and the overnight crossings to Palermo and Cagliari sail in the evening and dock at breakfast time. Island sailings are far more frequent from Easter to October, and the Aeolian, Pontine and Amalfi Coast fast boats are summer-only; rough weather in winter cancels hydrofoils fairly often, when the slower car ferries usually still run. If you are taking a car to Sicily or Sardinia, book well ahead in August.

half.name: Pompeii
half.blurb: The Roman city buried by Vesuvius in AD 79, its streets, frescoes, and plaster casts frozen mid-life.

half.name: Herculaneum
half.blurb: A smaller, better-preserved Vesuvian town where wooden beams and upper floors still survive.

half.name: Mount Vesuvius
half.blurb: Hike to the crater rim of the volcano that destroyed Pompeii for panoramic Bay of Naples views.

half.name: Caserta
half.blurb: The colossal Royal Palace of Caserta dazzles with its baroque staircase and fountain-lined gardens.

full.name: Capri
full.blurb: A glamorous island of dramatic cliffs, the shimmering Blue Grotto, and chic piazzetta cafes.

full.name: Amalfi Coast
full.blurb: Cliff-clinging villages like Positano and Amalfi strung along one of Europe's most scenic coastlines.

full.name: Sorrento
full.blurb: A clifftop resort town of lemon groves and bay views, the classic gateway to the Amalfi Coast.

full.name: Ischia
full.blurb: A green volcanic island known for thermal spa gardens, beaches, and the Aragonese Castle.

full.name: Paestum
full.blurb: Three remarkably intact Greek temples standing amid the ruins of an ancient Magna Graecia city.
